messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Vinh

Vinh was forty-four when the mugging happened, a night-shift nurse at a county hospital in a mid-sized city, steady in his work and married to his wife of sixteen years. On a Tuesday in March, he had finished his shift at eleven and decided to take a shortcut through the parking garage to his car rather than use the main corridor. The garage was poorly lit, and as he walked toward his vehicle on the third level, two men emerged from behind a concrete pillar. The first grabbed him from behind, wrenching his left arm upward, while the second punched him in the ribs and face. They took his wallet, his phone, his watch—the whole encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds, though Vinh would later describe it as feeling timeless. What stayed with him most viscerally was the moment he saw the first man's face clearly in the fluorescent light as they fled: a flash of features, an expression of cold calculation, burned into his mind with photographic precision. When the memory returned—and it returned constantly in those first weeks—Vinh experienced it not as narrative but as a series of still images, each one vivid and intrusive. He felt the phantom ache in his ribs where the punch had landed, a dull throb that would bloom across his chest whenever the images surfaced, as though his body were reliving the violence independently of his conscious mind.

In the weeks after the assault, Vinh became convinced that something about him had invited the attack. He replayed the moment endlessly: had he walked too slowly, signaling vulnerability? Had something in his bearing marked him as an easy target? He had come to believe that there was an intrinsic fault in how he moved through the world, a visible flaw that predators could sense. This conviction that he had somehow caused his own victimization began to reshape how he understood his future. Nothing good can happen to me anymore, he told himself. The attack was not a random tragedy but a revelation of a deeper truth about his life—that he was fundamentally unsafe, fundamentally flawed, and that no amount of caution could undo what he now was. Because he was certain that danger followed him, that his very presence attracted it, he began to adopt strategies designed to render himself invisible or untraceable. He installed a mirror on the dashboard of his car and checked it obsessively at red lights, watching for vehicles that might be tracking him. During his shifts at the hospital, he positioned himself so he could see the entrance to every room, and when he sat in the break room, he always chose the seat with the clearest view of the door and the fewest people behind him—a calculation so automatic that his colleagues began to notice he was always the last to arrive and the first to leave, never relaxing into the rhythm of shared meals.

The threat monitoring became relentless. Vinh found himself unable to sleep; his mind would race through scenarios of re-attack, and when exhaustion finally pulled him under, he would jolt awake at the slightest sound, his heart hammering. He frequently looked behind him when walking through corridors or parking lots, a habit so ingrained that it felt less like a conscious check and more like a necessary part of his sensory apparatus. To manage the anxiety that threatened to overwhelm him, he kept his mind constantly occupied—listening to podcasts during his commute, watching videos on his phone during breaks, anything to prevent the silence in which the images might surface. Yet the more he tried to distract himself, the more insistently the memories returned. The photographic vividness of the assault seemed to intensify whenever he was most vigilant, as though his heightened threat detection was actually amplifying the sensory precision of the trauma. The images would come unbidden, each one accompanied by the physical pain, and in those moments his conviction that he was fundamentally marked for suffering would deepen. He had come to see his hypervigilance not as a symptom but as a necessary adaptation to a world that had revealed itself to be irredeemably hostile.

Six months after the mugging, Vinh's marriage had begun to fracture under the weight of his vigilance. His wife found him distant, preoccupied, always checking mirrors and exits, never fully present. He had taken to avoiding the hospital parking garage entirely, using a longer route that added twenty minutes to his commute, and he had stopped going to the grocery store at night, asking his wife to do the shopping instead. The avoidance had begun to spread: he no longer attended his monthly poker game with friends, no longer took walks in the neighborhood where he and his wife had lived for over a decade. What frightened him most was not the possibility of another attack but the certainty he now carried that his life had fundamentally ended on that Tuesday night in March, and that everything since had been merely the prolonged aftermath of a death that had already occurred. It was only when his wife finally insisted that he see someone, when she told him she could no longer bear to live with the ghost of the man she had married, that Vinh finally made an appointment. He came to the first session exhausted, his eyes hollow, still checking the room's exits before sitting down, and when asked what he hoped might change, he could only shake his head. He was not certain that change was possible, or even that he deserved it.
